title: The CSS Box Model
summary: CSS treats each page part like a box. A box has content, padding, a border and margin.
introduction: CSS treats each page part like a box. A box has content, padding, a border and margin. Imagine a gift in a box: the gift is the content, and the space around it is padding. Learn which kind of space to change.
learningObjectives: Identify content, padding, border and margin on any element
Calculate an element's rendered size under content-box and border-box
Explain margin collapsing and use the shorthand spacing properties

blocks.text: Every element generates a rectangular box with four layers, from the inside out. The **content** area holds the text or the child elements. **Padding** is space inside the border, between the content and the edge. The **border** is the edge itself, visible once it has a style and a colour. The **margin** is space outside the border that keeps neighbouring boxes apart. A background paints the content and padding areas (and sits underneath the border), never the margin.

blocks.content: Light blue: content and padding. Blue edge: border. White around it: margin.

blocks.text: How wide is the box really?

By default (`box-sizing: content-box`) the `width` property sets the width of the *content area only*. Padding and border are added on the outside, so the card above is not 300px wide on screen but 300 + 20 + 20 + 4 + 4 = **348px**, and with its margins it claims 396px of its parent. This is the single most common source of layout surprises, which is why the alternative model exists.

blocks.title: The same declarations under both models
Rendered widths
blocks.content:
content-box: content 300px, padding 40px, border 8px  -> 348px wide
border-box:  content 252px, padding 40px, border 8px  -> 300px wide

blocks.text: `border-box` matches how people think ("make it 300px wide" means the whole visible box), so nearly every project starts with a reset that applies it to every element, including the `::before` and `::after` pseudo-elements:

blocks.title: 100% plus padding overflows
blocks.text: A box with `width: 100%` and `padding: 1rem` under the default `content-box` model is wider than its parent by 2rem, which produces a horizontal scrollbar or a box poking out on the right. Either apply the `border-box` reset above, or leave `width` at its default `auto`, which already fills the parent and makes room for padding.

`margin` and `padding` accept one to four values, assigned clockwise from the top: top, right, bottom, left. Two values mean vertical then horizontal; three mean top, horizontal, bottom. Margins may be negative (to pull an element towards or over a neighbour); padding may not. The special value `auto` on left and right margins absorbs the free space equally, which is how `margin: 0 auto` centres a block that has a width.

blocks.content: A centred card with uneven padding.

blocks.text: When the vertical margins of two block boxes touch, they **collapse** into one margin equal to the larger of the two, not their sum. A paragraph with `margin-bottom: 24px` followed by one with `margin-top: 16px` leaves 24px between them. Margins also collapse between a parent and its first or last child when no padding, border or content separates them, which is why a heading's top margin can appear *outside* the box that contains it. Horizontal margins never collapse, and neither do the margins of flex or grid items.

blocks.text: Collapsing is usually helpful: it keeps the space between paragraphs consistent whatever their order. When it gets in the way, give the parent some padding or a border, set `display: flow-root` on it, or lay the children out with flexbox or grid and use `gap` for spacing, where margins do not collapse at all. Many stylesheets also keep things predictable by using margins in one direction only, such as `margin-bottom` on every block.
Inspecting the box in developer tools

Select any element in the *Elements* (or *Inspector*) panel and open the *Computed* tab: the diagram shows the content size in the middle with padding, border and margin around it, and you can hover each layer to highlight it on the page. Hovering an element in the page with the inspector active uses the same colours: blue for content, green for padding, orange for margin. When something is wider than it should be, this view tells you which layer is responsible in seconds.

blocks.title: Logical properties
blocks.text: `margin-block: 1rem` sets the top and bottom margins and `padding-inline: 1rem` the left and right padding, in horizontal writing. These *logical* properties follow the writing direction, so a layout built with them works unchanged for right-to-left languages. All current browsers support them; you will see them in modern stylesheets alongside the physical `margin-top` style.

questions.question: Under the default `content-box` model, how wide on screen is a box with `width: 200px`, `padding: 10px` and `border: 5px solid`?
questions.explanation: Padding and border are added on both sides: 200 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 5 = 230px. With `border-box` the answer would be 200px.

questions.question: Left and right margins between neighbouring inline-block elements collapse into one.
questions.explanation: Only vertical margins of block boxes collapse. Horizontal margins always add up.
